breaking.headline: Flights recovering: FAA expects full schedules by late Sunday after ground stop
breaking.fact: FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said Saturday that U.S. airline schedules should be largely back to normal by late Sunday, after Friday’s nationwide ground stop — the longest in 25 years — and more than 15,000 cancellations Friday and Saturday. About 1,390 Sunday flights were already canceled Sunday morning, with Dallas-Fort Worth, O’Hare and JFK hit hardest. Officials blame an L3Harris contractor’s router work during a copper-to-fiber upgrade that overloaded communications at 17 of 22 air-traffic control centers; there is no sign of a cyberattack.

breaking.headline: U.S. loses measles elimination status after 26 years
breaking.fact: A Pan American Health Organization panel has determined the U.S. no longer qualifies as having eliminated measles, ending a status held since 2000, after the same strain circulated uninterrupted for more than a year. The CDC has tallied 5,412 cases in 2026 — the most since 1991 — with at least 10 deaths, and cases confirmed in 45 states. The formal announcement is expected Tuesday, Nov. 17.

breaking.headline: Houthis take control of Bab el-Mandeb as Yemeni forces pull back
breaking.fact: Yemen’s Southern Armed Forces announced Sunday they are withdrawing from Dhubab Airport and the Bab el-Mandeb area toward Aden, leaving the Iran-aligned Houthis in control of the strait overlooking one of the world’s busiest shipping chokepoints, the Red Sea–Suez route for Asia-to-Europe trade. The move ends a six-week government counteroffensive; no closure has been announced and vessels are still passing through.

breaking.headline: U.S. floated NATO-for-Donbas swap, Zelenskyy says
breaking.fact: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that U.S. negotiators asked whether Ukraine would withdraw from the Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership — the first time the question has been raised in the talks. Kyiv will not cede territory, he said, but would put a comprehensive security package to a national referendum. The Abu Dhabi round ended Wednesday without a breakthrough, though the sides agreed to swap more than 1,000 prisoners.

weekInBrief.headline: IEA: oil market swings back to surplus in the fourth quarter
weekInBrief.body: The International Energy Agency’s Nov. 13 Oil Market Report says the global oil market will return to surplus in the final quarter of 2026 as recovering supply outpaces demand — world supply rose 2.3 million barrels a day in October to 105.4 million — even as Washington’s blockade keeps Iranian crude off the market. Brent settled Friday at $95.84 and WTI at $88.56, both down about 2.5% for a second straight week.

weekInBrief.headline: Supreme Court to rule on Trump’s border asylum shutdown
weekInBrief.body: The justices agreed Friday to decide whether President Trump’s Jan. 20, 2025 proclamation barring asylum at the southern border is lawful, taking up Mullin v. RAICES after two lower courts found the policy illegal. Arguments are expected in spring 2027 with a ruling by the end of June; the shutdown stays in force meanwhile.

weekInBrief.headline: Lutnick and Huang agree to testify on Nvidia chip exports
weekInBrief.body: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify voluntarily before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10 on Nvidia chip exports to China and the Megaspeed investigation; former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned Nov. 11, was asked to appear Dec. 3 and has agreed to testify before House committees before Thanksgiving. The inquiry follows reports that more than $3 billion in Chinese AI projects run on restricted Nvidia chips.

weekInBrief.headline: COP31 grapples with the loss of the 1.5°C goal
weekInBrief.body: At the midpoint of the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, negotiators are split over what to do with the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C target after the UN declared a breach imminent and unavoidable: frontline states want the final deal to reaffirm it and commit to returning below it, while other blocs are pressing to drop it. New UN data puts the best-case warming outcome at 1.7–1.8°C.

items.headline: Latest from the Strait
items.body: CENTCOM said Saturday that more than 1.7 billion barrels of crude have now moved through the strait under U.S. protection, with F-16s flying patrols over the waterway. Iran answered with a fresh round of claims: its navy said another tanker struck a mine east of the strait on Friday, the Revolutionary Guard said it downed a U.S. MQ-1C drone over Qeshm Island, and Iranian state media said six attack drones targeted a U.S. radar site in Bahrain overnight. None of it is independently verified, and the Institute for the Study of War notes there are still no signs Iran has re-mined the southern route, which CENTCOM demined in August. On oil, that flow contrasts with a blockade that CENTCOM says has now prevented more than $25 billion in Iranian crude exports — non-Iranian oil is getting through in volume while Iranian oil is still shut out.

space.headline: Starship’s booster loss traced to engine trouble; the catch still stands as a first
space.body: SpaceX says preliminary indications point to a low-fuel-mass warning that ended the Super Heavy booster’s boostback burn early, and Elon Musk said slight engine underperformance was the reason Booster 22 diverted and exploded over the Gulf on Friday. The history stands regardless: Ship 42 was caught by the tower’s arms Saturday at 3:20 p.m. CT after 14 orbits and 26 Starlink V3 deployments — the first upper-stage catch ever — and SpaceX shares slipped to $136.25 after hours.

space.headline: CERN finds evidence of a one-in-ten-billion particle decay after 40 years
space.body: Physicists at CERN’s LHCb experiment have found the first single-experiment evidence for a neutral B meson decaying into two muons — a process predicted to happen only about once in every 10 billion beauty-particle decays, after a search running since the 1980s. The signal reaches 3.2 sigma, strong enough to call evidence but short of the five-sigma bar for a discovery; the result agrees with the Standard Model and tightens the hunt for new particles.

space.headline: Europe’s summer heat killed an estimated 50,391 people in its cities
space.body: A study in Nature Health estimates 50,391 heat-related excess deaths across 854 European cities during June–August 2026 — the highest toll on record, nearly double the summers of 2022 and 2003 — with about two-thirds attributable to human-caused climate change. Summer 2026 was the third-hottest on record for Europe and the hottest ever for western Europe; nearly a third of the deaths fell in a June 17–July 1 heat wave.

space.headline: Climate change is reshaping brain health, researchers warn
space.body: A report from the Neuro Climate Working Group, built by 50 global experts over two years, finds extreme heat, air pollution and wildfire smoke are harming cognition, mental health and neurodevelopment — and contributing to dementia risk: more than a quarter of dementia deaths in 2023 were attributable to air pollution, now the first environmental risk factor in the WHO’s dementia prevention guidelines. The authors call brain health ‘the blind spot of climate policy.’

apod.title: Leonid Meteors Through Orion
apod.credit: Luo Hongyang — NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day, November 15, 2026
apod.explanation: The 2022 Leonids streak across Orion over Hainan, China, looking out over the South China Sea — meteor trails captured over a few hours were layered onto a foreground shot of two stargazers. The Leonids peak in mid-November every year and peak again this week, with Mars glowing red near the top of the frame.
